text: Every running program on Linux becomes a process, tracked by a unique number called a PID. A single machine might have hundreds of processes running at once — the SSH daemon, a web server, a database, plus background system processes. The very first process the kernel starts at boot gets PID 1, and on a modern Linux system, that process is systemd.

ps aux lists every process on the system, showing the user running it, its PID, resource usage, and the command itself. For a live, constantly-updating view instead of a single snapshot, top, or the friendlier htop if it's installed, shows the same data refreshing in real time — the first place to look when a server feels slow.

When a process needs to stop, you send it a signal and let it decide how to react. Plain kill sends SIGTERM, a polite request — a well-behaved process catches it, closes its files and connections cleanly, and exits on its own terms. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, an unconditional, immediate kill with no chance to clean up. Always try SIGTERM first.

A service, or daemon, is a process meant to run continuously in the background, like sshd or nginx. systemd manages every service through the same handful of commands: systemctl status tells you if it's running and whether it starts on boot, start, stop, and restart control it immediately, and enable or disable control whether it survives a reboot.

Older Linux distributions managed services with SysVinit, which started them one at a time, in a fixed order, using inconsistent shell scripts. systemd replaced it almost everywhere because it starts independent services in parallel, tracks dependencies between them explicitly, and describes every service with one consistent unit file instead of a bespoke script.

That status-then-start-or-restart rhythm is something you'll use constantly once you're administering real servers, including every cloud VM ahead in this course.
